course_description:
A detailed study of Greek literary and historical texts chosen by the Course Coordinator.

GREK3002 is an advanced course in Ancient Greek Language and Literature with 2 hours of class one day a week.

In Semester 2 of 2026 we will study Book I and Book XXIV of the Iliad , the opening and closing of Homer’s masterpiece. Students will read, translate, and critically discuss around 100 lines per week over the course of the semester. By studying this foundational epic poem in its original language, and in its original contexts, students will develop an in-depth understanding of archaic Greek culture and its conception of the human and of human society. They will also gain an appreciation of the linguistic and formal qualities that make Homeric poetry so distinct, and the difficulties and opportunities such features present to the translator.

Before each weekly two-hour class, you are expected to prepare a pre-determined amount of text translation and discussion, and develop a critical awareness of major points of grammar, syntax, and style in the prepared material.. Regular preparation, participation and attendance are expected .

course_aims: This course aims to read Books 1 and 24 of Homer’s Iliad in a critical manner. Attention will be given to the language, grammar, and artistic construction of the text, and how these contribute to the poetic whole of the Iliad .

learning_outcomes.description: Students will develop advanced translation skills from ancient Greek into English by reading a wider range of unadapted ancient Greek poetry.
Students will develop advanced skills in the critical evaluation of ancient Greek literature, using their developing linguistic expertise to open up larger thematic and historical issues.

Students will develop a deep understanding of the oldest and most influential of ancient Greek literary genres, including not only its peculiar dialect, metre, and habits of expression, but also its larger habits of thought.
Students will develop an understanding of the political, social, and cultural context of the production, dissemination, and reception of Homeric poetry.
Students will develop the ability to evaluate ethically issues and questions raised by the text(s) pertaining to freedom, violence, and justice.

Students will have the opportunity to demonstrate transferable workplace skills through class activities and assessment tasks which develop advanced written and verbal communication tasks, advanced problem solving, leadership, and critical thinking skills.

assessment_details.title: Research Essay
assessment_details.due_date: 27/10/2026 2:00 pm Submit via turnitin as instructed on Blackboard
assessment_details.task_description: Students are required to write a critical evaluation essay based on the text(s) set for analysis. Students are also required to provide their own English translations of the Greek text(s). This essay requires you to demonstrate your understanding of the Greek text(s) set for analysis. It does not require extensive reading of modern sources outside the recommended reading list on Blackboard, unless you come across something relevant which you use critically in your analysis. Please Note: A word count that is within ±10% of the set length (word limit) is acceptable. A word count that is outside these 10% will receive a proportionate penalty and will be graded against the grading criteria. Essay Questions and further details will be made available on Blackboard, and students will have the opportunity to practice and discuss the type of analysis required in class before the submission date. Fabrication or misrepresentation of sources is considered a breach of academic integrity and may be referred for academic misconduct, regardless of performance in other criteria. This includes but is not limited to: citing non-existent sources, attributing false quotes to real sources, or not including accurate page numbers. assessment_details.task_description: Each week, students will be expected to prepare about 100 lines of Greek, and to bring three (at least!) queries about the language they have encountered. They must participate actively in group discussion of the text and its meaning. Each student will also be assigned a number of lines within that 100-line section, which they must be ready to present on, both translating for the class and leading a short discussion. Students will also be required to do a 5 min presentation on a scholarly publication on the Iliad . Further information will be provided on Blackboard and in class.
